title: Shared Ancestor via Parent Links
statement:
A binary tree has nodes numbered 0 to n − 1. You do not get the root or any child links. You only get parent, where parent[i] is the parent of node i, and -1 marks the root. This is like a DOM node where you can only follow parentNode.

Given two different nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree. A node counts as being in its own subtree, so if p is above q, the answer is p.

(The original version passes node objects with a parent field. Here the parent array plays that role and nodes are referred to by index.)

examples.why: 3 climbs 1 → 0 and 5 climbs 2 → 0. The first node both paths reach is the root.
1 is the parent of 4, so 1 itself is the shared ancestor.
The root is node 1, not node 0. 4 sits two levels deeper than 0, so the two climbs must be lined up before they meet at 2.

constraints: parent describes one binary tree with exactly one -1
hints: Walk from p to the root and remember every node you pass. What does the first remembered node on q's walk tell you?
That uses O(depth) memory. If p and q were at the same depth, you could climb them together until they land on the same node.
Two pointers: each climbs one step at a time, and when one falls off the root it restarts at the other's start node. Both then travel the same total distance and meet exactly at the shared ancestor.

explain.intuition:
Climbing from a node to the root gives its full list of ancestors. The answer is the first node on q's climb that also appears on p's climb. A set does that in O(depth) space.

To drop the set, notice this is the same puzzle as two linked lists that merge: each climb is a list ending at the root, and the lists join at the shared ancestor. Let pointer a start at p and b at q. When a pointer runs off the root, send it to the other start node. After the switch, both have walked depth(p) + depth(q) steps minus the shared tail, so they arrive at the meeting node on the same step, without ever computing depths.
steps: While a ≠ b: move a to parent[a], or to q if a was the root.
Likewise move b to parent[b], or to p if b was the root.
pitfalls: Assuming node 0 is the root. The root is whichever node has -1, as in the third example.
Climbing both pointers in lock step without lining up depths first. They pass each other and never meet.
Forgetting that a node can be its own ancestor. When p is above q, the answer is p, not p's parent.

complexity.time: O(h), where h is the tree height

solutions.title: Remember p's ancestors
solutions.idea: Store every node on p's climb in a set, then climb from q until you hit one.

solutions.title: Line up the depths
solutions.idea: Measure both depths, lift the deeper node by the difference, then climb both together until they coincide.

solutions.title: Two pointers that swap starts
solutions.idea: Like finding where two linked lists merge: when a pointer passes the root it restarts at the other node, so both cover the same distance.

followups: Why does the swap version terminate even when p is an ancestor of q?
You must answer many (p, q) queries on the same tree. How would binary lifting help?
